In Domesday Book (1086) and in the Pipe Rolls of the reign of Henry II., York appears throughout as Everwich or Eurwic, and Yorkshire as Everwichsciy or Eurvic-scyre ; Layamon, not liking Danish barbarisms, always refers to it as Eouerwike or Euerwic, while Euerwik, Euerwyc, Euerwyk and Euerwic are the spellings of the name in the metrical chronicle of Robert of Gloucester (fl. 1260-1300).

Eburacum—Cair Eborauc —Eoforwic—Ioforvik—York: here, indeed, is a palimpsest, over-written by the hands of many men, speaking many tongues; and at the same time the name, when all its changeful history has been recorded, stands before us as an ever-during symbol of the play of the great national forces which, in the revolution of the years, and through the agencies of peace and war, have built up the England that we know to-day.

-(H)ALL. Occurs in Beal, Burnsall, Campsall, Elmsall, Gomersal, Hensall, Killinghall, Loversall, Newhall, Roall, Sicklinghall, Tyersall, Worrall ; also in the earlier forms of Skellow, Snaygill, snydale, Stancill, Wighill, Wilsill; perhaps also in Cattal, Kiddall, Painley. It is possible that in Sicklinghall and Newhall the termination -hall or -all goes back to O.E. hall, heall=a large covered building, palace, hall, royal residence. But in the remaining names the termination is probably O.E. halh, healh =a corner, nook, heel of land, cognate to Greek xéAzos = a fold, hollow, creek. The word is used in O.E. asa translation of the Latin angulus. The full termination halk is seen in Bede’s Streaneshalh = Whitby—a name which survives in the place-name Strensall, near York.

But in the remaining names the termination is probably O.E. halh, healh =a corner, nook, heel of land, cognate to Greek xéAzos = a fold, hollow, creek. The word is used in O.E. asa translation of the Latin angulus. The full termination halk is seen in Bede’s Streaneshalh = Whitby—a name which survives in the place-name Strensall, near York.

The word thorp occurs in O.E. but is much more common in O.N., and in English place-names it is most often met with in the Scandinavian districts of England An examination of the above list of names shows that the first element in them is usually Scandinavian.

The word thorp is also cognate to the Cymric fref, a village, found in the Welsh place-name Trefriw. The termination is frequently found in Danish place-names, more rarely in Norwegian, and more rarely still in Icelandic.

It is probable that the Bicker- of Bickerton is another form of the Becker which appears in Beckering (Lincs.), Beckermonds (Yorks.), and Beckermet (Cumberland), and that both go back to O.N. bekkjar, the gen. sing. of bekkr=a stream, beck, cf. the O.N. compound bekkjarkvern =a water-mill. The meaning of Bickerton is, accordingly, “‘the enclosure by the water.”

Cletherum (Jetferys Top. survey (17721): This is a difficult name, and it is evident from the forms which appear above that the termination -holme is not original. The D.B. form of the name, Cludun, if any reliance is to be placed upon it, is apparently a weakened form of O.E. Cludum, the dat. pl. of O.F. clid=a rock, hill. This would give us ‘among the rocks,’ or ‘ on the hills’ as the meaning of Clotherholme.

O.F. clid=a rock, hill. This would give us ‘among the rocks,’ or ‘ on the hills’ as the meaning of Clotherholme. But it is probable that the M.E. forms Cluderum, Clutherum, Clotherun: are connected with the dialect word clitter (of which clatter and clutter are variant forms), meaning ‘a pile of loose stones, debris from the side of a hill’ (see Wright’s Dialect Dictionary, ‘ Clitter’). Early forms of cltéer or clittey are not found, but whether of English or Scandinavian origin, its dative plural would end in -wm; and for this -wm has been substituted, in the place-name Clotherholme, the O.N. termination holmr, 1.¢., a piece of land surrounded or almost surrounded by water.

I am disposed to think that the original form of the termination was ergh (=a shieling, dairy-farm), from the Gaelic aerg, airigh, which was introduced into O.N. and appears commonly in the Scandinavian place-names of Caithness (¢.g., Asgrimserg, mentioned in the Orkneyingasaga), and in the Norse names of the English Lake-district (e.g., Mansergh, Sizergh, Ninesergh). In such a form as Goualacres we see the O.E. ecer= a field, taking the place of the earlier evgh, while in Guldecar and the modern Golcar, evgh has given place to M.E. ker, Mod. E. car, ~from O.N. kiavr=a swampy copse. The original meaning of Golcar was accordingly “‘ the dairy-farm of the Norseman Guthlaug,”’ (Guthlaugsairigh or Guthlaugsergh).

The spelling Heawic in Birch’s Cartularium makes it fairly certain that Hewick derives its name from O.E. héah, héh=high, and O.E.. wic=a dwelling-place, village. The meaning is accordingly “‘ the dwelling-place on high ground.” In the case of Copt Hewick, the D.B. form Hadewic would lead us to suppose that it is from O.E. Haddanwic =the village of Hadda; but in the absence of other forms with medial d, the D.B. spelling carries little weight, and the probability is that the two Hewicks are identical in origin. The word Copt, which we meet with again in Copt Hall (Essex), and Copt Oak (Leics.), is from O.E. copped = polled, lopped, pollarded, so that Copt Hewick is “the village on high ground by the pollard-trees”’; cf. to than coppedan thorne = to the pollard thorn (B.C.S., 740).

The first element in the name Keswick is probably Anglian- English cése, West Saxon ciese, cjse=cheese. In Anglo-Danish districts O.E. c before front vowels was frequently not palatalised to ch, and the Cumberland word hesvat=cheese-vat, and the northern dialects word keslip or keslop =rennet, are other instances of this absence of palatisation of Anglian cése. With the dropping of the inflectional e in Kesewic, the long in O.E. cése became shortened before the two consonants, and the resultant form is Keswick. The meaning of Keswick is accordingly “ the cheese farm,” or: “‘the dairy farm.”

There is some variation in the termination of this name, but the form in -den, from O.E. denu=a valley, seems to have been the original one, and it remained in use as late as the nineteenth century. The first element in the name is probably the O.E. personal name Hlothhere, which occurs in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle and, as Lothere, in the place-name Lotheresleh of Kemble’s Codex (No. 1223). The form Letheresden shows confusion between the two O.E. names Hlothhere and Leodhere, from the latter of which comes the place- name Letherhead; similar confusion arose in Germany between the forms Hlodhar and Liuthar, which are cognate with the O.E. Hlothhere and Leodhere respectively. See Lotherton.

This is a difficult name, and the D.B. form Napars does not seem very helpful. It is probable that the Naphay of Archbishop Gray’s Register is the most primitive of the forms given above, and [ think it at least possible that the constituent elements of Naphay are O.E. nép from Lat. napus =a turnip, and O.E. heg, haga =an enclosure. The long vowel in nép would undergo shortening before the two consonants, and the resultant M.E. form would be Naphay, later Nappay. If this derivation of Nappa is correct, the meaning of the name is “ the turnip field.”

(see Kemble’s Codex, No. 652), and is found in M.E. side by side with pofler, poplar, from the Old French poplier. Risington (K.I., 359 [1285-1316]). The form Rzsington is without support, and the probability is that Rosingion is the true M.E. form. I am disposed to connect the name with the Teutonic root hros =a horse, which is changed to hors in O.E., but appears as hross in O.N., hros in Old Saxon and Old High German, and vos in Old Frisian.

The famous O.E. name Horsa and the Icelandic names Hrosskill and Hrossbjérn show clearly that the word was often used as a personal name, and Rossington may therefore be “the enclosure of the family of a Scandinavian called Hrossi or Hrosskill, or of a German called Hroso or Roso.”

Streetthorpe is a corruption of an earlier Que, in which the first element is the Scandinavian personal name Styrr. There was a Stir or Styrr who was “ major domus”’ to King Harthacnut in the eleventh century, while the compound forms Styrbjorn, (otyumeat, and Styrcat are found in O\B.-and O.N. records, — the meaning of Streetthorpe is accordingly “the village of Styrr.”. In Norway the name Styrr enters into the formation of the place-names Styrsrud, Styrsvik, and Styrseng ; see Rygh, of. cit., p. 238-9.

Stub in Dorsetshire appears as Styb in Kemble’s Codex (No. 447), and indicates that the origin of the place-name Stub or Stubbs is O.E. stybb, stubb =a stump of a tree, a stub. Stubbs means accord- ingly: “ the tree-stumps,”’ 7.e., a piece of land once forest, but-on Which: the trees have been felled*close to the ground. The name Walden in Stubbs Walden has developed out of the. family name Waldyng, Walding, borne by the lords of the manor of Stubbs in the thirteenth century (see Pontefract Chartulary, pp. 322 ., 327).

Whistan (P.T. [1379]). The early spellings of Whiston vary considerably and make the etymological investigation of the name somewhat difficult. The name may mean “ the white stone”’ or “ the wide stone.” If the former rendering is correct, Whiston goes back to O.E. Hwitanstan, or et thém hwitan stdne=at the white stone; cf. Hwitanstan in Kemble’s Codex (No. 431). But the form Wrdestan in D.B., and Wythstan in Archbishop Giffard’s Register seem to indicate that the first element is O.N. vithy or O.E. wid =wide ; and the fact that the Wydecumb of Kemble’s Codex (No. 375) has become Whitcombe (Dorset) shows that a substitution of ‘white’ for ‘wide’ is a possibility.

The ordinary O.E. word for a sheaf of corn was vip, but the torm rypa or ripa, with short vowel, is found in the Psalteriwm Latino-Saxonicum. This would give us " the meadow where the sheaves stand," or " the meadow where corn is reaped," as the meaning of Ripley. The popular derivation of Ripon from the Latin fa is highly improbable, for there is no evidence at all that this word was ever in use in either Celtic or Old English. It is much more likely that Ripon is from an O.E. word 1p, rip, which appears in O.E. charters, and is closely allied to the Frisian word rife, meaning 'a border, edge, shore.' In a Kentish charter of the year 740 there occurs the following phrase: ad silbam [sic] qui appellatur ripp et ad terminos suthsaxoniae (K.C.D., 86), which is repeated in a charter of the following year (K.C.D., 1003), with the form Rip for ripp. From this it is evident that Riip or Ripp is the name of a wood, and the fact that it lay close to the boundary of the South-Saxon territory. favours the view that the 'silva qui appellatur ripp' may be interpreted ' the border wood.' Accepting this derivation, we may regard Ripon as taking its name from O.E. 1m ripum = on the borders. Bede's spelling of the name does not conflict with this view ; confusion between an initial fy and 7 is not unusual in O.E., and we find O.E. réaf (=plunder) spelt hréaf, O.E. risc (=a rush) spelt hrisc, and O.E. ripan (=to reap) spelt hripan. But it is also possible that a tribal name lurks in Ripon, and that Bede's phrase, 7m Hrypum, may have meant 'among the people called Hrype or Hrypas.'
